newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan considers cut in bread prices.
newsitem.headline: Jordan considers cut in bread prices.

text.p: Prompted by softer world grain prices, Jordan is considering plans to lower bread prices two months after steep IMF-approved rises sparked civil unrest, officials and traders said on Friday.

Officials said Prime Minister Abdul Karim al-Kabariti is considering a substantial reduction in bread prices prompted by recent cheaper wheat purchases with some of the heat may be going out of world grain prices, lately at historic highs.
"They are basing an expected decision on lowering bread prices on the recent drop in wheat prices," said one official.
The decision to almost double bread prices in August in line with IMF-agreed economic reforms led to the worst civil unrest since riots in 1989, also sparked by government price rises.

A senior official said any price drop "would reflect the recent downward trend in world wheat prices," but did not say how much. He hinted the move could be taken before parliament reconvenes after a summer recess in November.

This would defuse the Islamist opposition's orchestrated attack on the government's handling of the unrest that shook the impoverished south and was widely blamed on declines in living standards since Jordan's 1994 peace treaty with Israel.
The government's bread prices are fixed at 180 fils (25 U.S. cents) and 220 fils (31 cents) per kilo (2.2 lbs) from 85 fils (12 cents) before the August price hike.
Since the riots Jordan has bought 140,000 tonnes of wheat at prices ranging from $191-206 per tonne, a nearly 25 percent drop from a high of $275 per tonne last May.

To cash in on current softer world wheat prices -- with prices fluctuating in the $170 per tonne range -- Jordan announced on Thursday a snap tender to buy 150,000 tonnes of U.S. high grade or equivalent origin wheat on October 15.

Grain traders say the government can comfortably take the decision, helped by success in eliminating bread waste used extensively as animal fodder. Figures show flour consumption since the controversial price hike has dropped 34 percent.
Animal fodder, solely imported by the state, also saw a drop in consumption after a 12 percent price hike that provided government coffers an extra six million dinars monthly.
Jordan's budget deficit -- ballooning due to the higher subsidy bill to over 100 million dinars -- was now under control, buttressed by extra soft loans, officials said.

Tackling the costly subsidies was key to the three-year International Monetary Fund-directed reform programme which Jordan began in 1996. The fund linked millions of dollars of aid to steps to liberalise the economy.
Bread is a staple food for Jordan's 4.2 million people who have a per capita gross domestic product of about $1,500 a year.
